title: Five Rules, One Target: The Trump Administration Is Rewriting Every Immigration Pathway Indians Use to Live in America
excerpt: H-1B placements face new scrutiny, Green Card wage floors are doubling, student visas will expire, and 100,000 H-4 spouses could lose work authorization — all by August.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Trump administration proposes comprehensive immigration restrictions affecting Indian professionals and students.
  • H-1B visa rules will tighten, impacting third-party placements and increasing costs for employers.
  • Green Card wage thresholds will double, potentially discouraging employer sponsorship for Indian applicants.
  • International students face fixed-period visas, ending the 'duration of status' system.
  • 100,000 H-4 spouses may lose work authorization due to new processing rules.
The Trump administration is preparing to roll out the most comprehensive set of immigration restrictions in years, with proposed and final rules targeting H-1B visas, Green Card applications, student visa pathways, and H-4 spousal work permits. If the changes take effect as planned — some as early as this month, others by August — they will reshape the lives of hundreds of thousands of Indian professionals, students, and their families in the United States. The proposals, outlined in the Unified Regulatory Agendas released by the Departments of Homeland Security, Labor, and State, touch virtually every pathway Indians use to work and study in America. ## H-1B: Tighter Rules for Outsourcing and Third-Party Placements A rule the Department of Homeland Security expects to publish in August would leave the annual H-1B cap unchanged at 85,000 but impose stricter requirements on third-party client-site placements — the staffing model that underpins much of India's IT services industry. Under the proposed rule, employers would need to demonstrate a genuine employer-employee relationship and verify that specialty occupation duties are being performed at each client site. Companies with prior violations would face heightened scrutiny. Firms with more than 50 U.S. employees where H-1B or L-1 holders make up over half the workforce would face additional fees — $4,000 per H-1B extension and $4,500 per L-1 extension — that currently apply only to initial petitions or employer changes. The timing is significant. Vice President JD Vance announced last week that the Department of Labor had launched "dozens of subpoenas and investigations" into H-1B visa fraud, and a federal judge recently struck down a separate Trump executive order imposing a $100,000 application fee. ## Green Cards: The Wage Floor Is Doubling The Department of Labor is drafting rules to raise the prevailing wage thresholds for H-1B and PERM labour certification cases — the first step in most employer-sponsored Green Card applications. The entry-level benchmark would jump from the 17th to the 34th percentile, with higher wage tiers increasing proportionally. > **"The DHS is expected to issue a final rule this month ending the "duration of status" system, which has allowed international students to remain in the U.S."** The practical effect: employers would need to pay significantly more to sponsor a foreign worker for permanent residency. For Indian applicants, who already face the longest Green Card backlog in the world — often exceeding a decade — the higher cost could push some employers to abandon sponsorship altogether. Additional PERM changes would tighten recruitment standards, introduce new rules around U.S. worker layoffs, and strengthen anti-discrimination compliance. ## Students: The End of 'Duration of Status' ![Green Card — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/4/49/2023_green_card_front.jpg) India sent 360,000 students to the United States in the 2024-25 academic year, accounting for nearly 31 per cent of all international enrolments — the largest single-country share. Those students are about to face a fundamental change in how their visas work. The DHS is expected to issue a final rule this month ending the "duration of status" system, which has allowed international students to remain in the U.S. as long as they maintain their academic programme requirements. Under the new rules, students would receive fixed-period visas and would need to apply for formal extensions — with the attendant fees, paperwork, and processing delays — to continue their studies. A separate proposal expected in early 2027 would restrict Optional Practical Training, the programme that allows graduates to work in the U.S. for up to three years in STEM fields. OPT has become the primary on-ramp for Indian students transitioning from university into the American workforce, and its restriction would narrow the pipeline considerably.

## H-4 Spouses: 100,000 Workers Could Lose Authorization Perhaps the most immediately consequential change involves the H-4 visa, held predominantly by spouses — overwhelmingly women — of Indian H-1B workers. A final rule expected later this month would end the automatic extension of Employment Authorization Documents, reversing a Biden-era policy that provided a 540-day safety net for applicants awaiting renewal. The arithmetic is simple and punishing. H-4 EAD holders can submit renewal applications no earlier than 180 days before expiry. USCIS processing regularly takes seven to ten months, and sometimes longer. Without the automatic extension, an estimated 100,000 Indian spouses could face gaps in work authorization — forced out of jobs they hold legally, not because their applications were denied, but because the government cannot process paperwork fast enough. Immigration attorneys have warned that the policy could force dual-income Indian families into single-earner status overnight, with cascading effects on mortgages, childcare, and financial planning. ## What It Means for the Diaspora None of these measures has taken effect yet. Several are proposed rules that require public comment periods before finalization. But together, they represent a clear signal: the administration intends to constrict every major pathway Indians use to live and work in the United States. For families navigating the system — the software engineer on an H-1B, the spouse on an H-4, the student on an F-1, the family waiting years for a Green Card — the changes are not abstract. They are a set of interlocking pressures that could turn a decade-long immigration journey into something even more uncertain. The public comment periods on the proposed rules may offer a window for advocacy. Immigration lawyers and community organizations are urging affected families to submit formal comments and engage with elected officials before the rules are finalized.
